text: This lab walks through one real scenario, pulling together everything this chapter has covered. The CMDB Health Dashboard for a mid-size environment shows a duplicate rate of forty percent on server CIs -- more than a third of server records are likely duplicating another record already in the table, while Completeness and Correctness both look fine.

The instinct is to jump straight to merging duplicates, but cleanup without fixing the cause just gets undone by the next Discovery run. Reviewing the Identification Rule for server CIs turns up the problem: it matches only on Host Name. In this environment, virtual machines routinely get renamed during promotion -- a VM built as TEMP-BUILD-04 becomes WEB-PROD-17 once it reaches production. Discovery finds no existing record with that new hostname and creates a brand-new CI instead of recognizing the machine it already had.

The fix is to stop relying on a value that can change. The hardware serial number, or for a VM the hypervisor-assigned instance UUID, gets added as the independent identifier, since it survives a rename. Host Name plus Domain stays as a secondary identifier. This change alone doesn't touch the existing forty percent -- it only stops new duplicates from this specific cause going forward.

With the rule fixed, duplicate detection is run against the server CI class, surfacing the likely-duplicate pairs the new rule would have caught the first time. Each pair is reviewed by hand to confirm a genuine match, then merged -- never deleted -- so Incident history, Change records, and relationships consolidate onto the single surviving CI.

The rule is fixed and the backlog is cleared, but that alone doesn't keep it fixed. The last step is naming a specific accountable owner -- a named lead on the Infrastructure Team -- as the CI-class data owner for server CIs, checking the duplicate-rate score on a quarterly cadence so the next version of this problem gets caught long before it reaches forty percent.

Diagnose the cause, fix the rule, clean up the backlog, then assign ownership -- in that order. That closes out this chapter. Next up, the course's final chapter opens with a capstone: modeling a real service from the ground up, using everything from CI classes through governance.
